title: Γεωργὸς καὶ ἀετός
part: The Farmer and the Eagle (Chambry 79 · Perry 296)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 79 (= Perry 296). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation ([ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γεωργὸς ἀετὸν εὑρὼν ἠγρευμένον, τὸ κάλλος αὐτοῦ θαυμάσας, ἀπέλυσεν αὐτὸν ἐλεύθερον.
sentences.tr: Geōrgos aeton heurōn ēgreumenon, to kallos autou thaumasas, apelysen auton eleutheron.
sentences.l: A farmer, having found an eagle that had been caught, having admired its beauty, released it free.
sentences.i: A farmer found an eagle that had been trapped, and admiring its beauty, let it go free.
sentences.n: ἠγρευμένον is the perfect passive participle of ἀγρεύω, 'take in hunting': not the catching but the state of being caught. ἐλεύθερον stands predicatively with the verb — he released it so that it was free.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ οὐκ ἄμοιρος αὐτῷ χάριτος κατεφάνη, ἀλλ’ ὑπὸ τεῖχος σαθρὸν καθήμενον ἰδών, προσπετάσας τοῖς ποσὶν ἦρε τὸ ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ φακιόλιον.
sentences.tr: Ho de ouk amoiros autōi charitos katephanē, all’ hypo teichos sathron kathēmenon idōn, prospetasas tois posin ēre to epi tēs kephalēs autou phakiolion.
sentences.l: But it showed itself not without a share of gratitude toward him, but, having seen him sitting beneath a crumbling wall, having spread its wings towards him, with its feet it took away the headcloth that was on his head.
sentences.i: But the eagle proved not ungrateful to him: seeing him sitting beneath a crumbling wall, it swooped down and carried off in its talons the cloth from his head.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἄμοιρος χάριτος is litotes, 'not without a share of gratitude'; χάρις is both the favour done and the thanks owed for it, and this fable needs both senses at once. προσπετάσας is from πετάννυμι, 'spread out' — properly 'having spread its wings towards him', which is a swoop. φακιόλιον, a cloth wound round the head, is a late word borrowed from Latin faciale; the Greek of this collection is not uniformly Attic.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἐξαναστὰς ἐδίωκε· τοῦτο δὲ ὁ ἀετὸς ἔρριψε.
sentences.tr: Ho de exanastas ediōke· touto de ho aetos erripse.
sentences.l: And he, having sprung up, was giving chase; and the eagle threw it down.
sentences.i: The man sprang up and gave chase; and the eagle dropped it.
sentences.n: The tenses do the work: the imperfect ἐδίωκε is a chase still going on, the aorist ἔρριψε the single act that ends it — and takes the man away from the wall.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἀναλαβόμενος αὐτὸ καὶ ὑποστρέψας εὗρε τὸ τεῖχος συμπεπτωκὸς ἔνθα ἐκάθητο, θαυμάσας τὴν ἀμοιβήν.
sentences.tr: Kai analabomenos auto kai hypostrepsas heure to teichos sympeptōkos entha ekathēto, thaumasas tēn amoibēn.
sentences.l: And having taken it up and having turned back, he found the wall fallen in where he had been sitting, marvelling at the recompense.
sentences.i: He picked it up, turned back, and found the wall collapsed where he had been sitting; and he marvelled at the return made him.
sentences.n: συμπεπτωκός is the perfect participle of συμπίπτω, 'fall in together': the collapse is over and its result stands. ἀμοιβή is what is given back in exchange — the χάρις of the second sentence, now paid. θαυμάσας repeats the participle of the opening line: he admired the bird's beauty, and now what the bird did.

sentences.t: Ὅτι τοὺς ἀγαθόν τι πεπονθότας ἔκ τινος ἀντευεργετεῖν χρή· [ὃ γὰρ ἀγαθὸν ποιήσεις, ἀντιδοθήσεταί σοι.]
sentences.tr: Hoti tous agathon ti peponthotas ek tinos anteuergetein chrē· [ho gar agathon poiēseis, antidothēsetai soi.]
sentences.l: That those who have received some good from someone must do good in return; [for whatever good you do will be given back to you.]
sentences.i: The story shows that those who have received some good from someone must do good in return; [for whatever good you do will be given back to you.]
sentences.n: A moral opening with a bare Ὅτι: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which simply begins 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. πάσχω, whose perfect participle is πεπονθότας, covers receiving as well as suffering — one verb for whatever is done to you, good or ill. The ἀντι- prefix runs through both halves (ἀντευεργετεῖν, ἀντιδοθήσεται): doing good back, given back. Chambry brackets the closing clause as an interpolation.
